newsitem.title: USA: Weather again threatens U.S shuttle landing.
newsitem.headline: Weather again threatens U.S shuttle landing.

text.p: Bad weather at NASA's Florida spaceport threatened to postpone the homecoming of the space shuttle Discovery for a second day running, officials said on Tuesday.
The $2 billion gliding spaceship was to touch down at the Kennedy Space Center at 7:08 a.m. EDT (1108 GMT), but there was a low cloud layer and a possibility of rain showers.
"We're not out of the woods yet on the weather," mission control's Dom Gorie informed the astronauts soon after they closed the shuttle's cargo bay doors in preparation for landing.

On Monday NASA waved off a anding attempt because of a chance for fog at the Florida runway. As it turned out, the predicted fog never materialized and blue skies would have greeted the returning astronauts.
The shuttle has only one landing opportunity on Tuesday in Florida, because NASA officials want the shuttle to touch down after sunrise. Landings in darkness are generally considered more risky.
Discovery's backup landing strip at Edwards Air Force Base in California would not be considered on Tuesday because of the additional $900,000 cost of transporting the orbiter back to Florida.
Although the shuttle had enough fuel and supplies to stay aloft until Thursday, it was expected to return to Earth on one coast or the other by Wednesday.

Discovery's crew of six enjoyed their extra day aloft on Monday by watching the Earth speed by 160 miles (256 km) below and scientists took the opportunity to cram in some last-minute observations with cargo bay instruments.

During the jam-packed mission the astronauts released and later recovered an ozone monitoring satellite, checked out a Japanese prototype space station robot arm, and pointed a small telescope at the receding comet Hale-Bopp.
